newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian state hopes to save rhino in outback.
newsitem.headline: Australian state hopes to save rhino in outback.

text.p: The Australian state of Queensland is hoping to persuade South African leader Nelson Mandela to back plans for an outback wilderness haven for the endangered rhinoceros.
The proposal aims to combine the need for sustainable development of Queensland's vast inland savannah with efforts to save the rhino, officials said on Wednesday.

A spokesman for Queensland Tourism Minister Bruce Davidson told Reuters the minister would meet South African officials during a trip to South Africa next week and hoped to meet President Mandela to discuss the project.
"The minister will be leaving next week and hopes to talk to Mr Mandela. If not, the minister will be talking to senior government officials about the project," he said.
He said the rhino project had tourist potential -- but preservation of the animal was the primary concern.

Only about 12,000 rhinos survive in southern Africa and Asia and numbers are being steadily eroded by poaching. Rhino horns are used in traditional Chinese medicine as an aphrodisiac and are also sought after for dagger handles in the Middle East.

Efforts to create the rhino sanctuary follow conservation studies of northern Australia's savannah lands under the government's cooperative research centres (CRC) scheme, which promotes industry-linked research and development.
A CRC spokesman said the savannahs of tropical northern Australia and south-west and central Africa had marked similarities in topography, climate and vegetation.

"With escalating pressures on rhino habitats in Africa for resettlement, agricultural and residential purposes, and with incessant poaching of the horn, these outback expanses offer a secure location to conserve and breed these unique species," he said.
The Queensland government has contributed A$10,000 (US$7,600) to the proposal, which is also being backed by a private company, Sanctuary Reserve Pty Ltd.

The CRC spokesman said initial research has identified areas which could host a rhino breeding and conservation sanctuary of up to 200,000 hectares (500,000 acres), inland from the tourist port of Cairns on Australia's east coast.

"By merging the cooperative research centre's mission of sustainable development of tropical savannahs with the urgent need to save the rhino, a highly successful conservation project is possible," the spokesman said.
The project would aim to be commercially viable through tourism, and was seen as providing employment in a remote and under-developed region.

The CRC spokesman said a project team was investigating the feasibility and requirements of quarantine, transport, permits, zoo certification, planning and design as well as veterinary care and supervision.
"A key element of the project will be ensuring that any ecological impact is minimised," he added.
Preliminary results were expected by September this year, followed by a full feasibility study of ecological, economic, social, cultural and design issues.
